 Mathematician Claims Riemann Hypothesis Proof
 Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic employee, says he used Claude to produce a proof of the 167-year-old problem.
 Updated on Nov. 20, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence 
 Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic employee, says he used Claude to produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem that remains unverified by experts. AI Illustration. Upload story photo > Live Poll
 Do you think AI will be a net positive for society?
 ▲ Yes ▼ No Mathematician Levent Alpöge posted a statement on his website on Friday claiming a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced with the help of Claude, a large language model. The proof was posted in the Lean programming language, which verifies the correctness of each argument.
 Why it matters
 The Riemann hypothesis, first proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, is considered the most famous open problem in mathematics. If verified, a machine-assisted proof would mark a notable test of how AI tools can contribute to advanced mathematical research.
 The claimed proof is written in Lean, which checks each argument for mathematical correctness rather than relying on informal review. Whether the formalization faithfully encodes the Riemann hypothesis, and whether the proof holds, remains to be confirmed by experts.
 The players
 Levent Alpöge
 Alpöge is a mathematician and employee at Anthropic, the AI company that develops Claude.
 Anthropic
 Anthropic is an artificial intelligence company that develops the Claude family of large language models.
 Bernhard Riemann
 Bernhard Riemann was a 19th-century German mathematician whose work on prime numbers and the zeta function gave rise to the Riemann hypothesis.
 The details
 Alpöge said he produced the proof working with Claude and posted it coded in Lean on his website. Lean verifies the mathematical correctness of each step, and experts are expected to check whether the hypothesis is properly coded and whether the proof is sound.
 Timeline
 1859: Bernhard Riemann first proposes the Riemann hypothesis.
 Friday, November 20, 2026: Alpöge posts his claimed proof on his website.
 The Tech Race
 The claim follows Riemann's 1859 proposal of the hypothesis, one of mathematics' longest-standing open questions. It positions AI-assisted formal proof as a new route into problems that have resisted human effort for more than a century and a half.
 For most readers the claim has no immediate effect, since it remains unverified. Its significance depends on whether formal verification tools built around AI can reliably settle long-standing problems that affect fields relying on prime number theory.
 The takeaway
 Claims of major mathematical proofs should be judged by independent verification, and formal languages like Lean are designed to make that checking possible. Readers should wait for expert review before treating the result as settled.
 What happens next
 Experts are expected to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded in Lean and whether the proof is correct; no date for that review has been given.
